1. WHAT WE FOUND

Nigeria is where the money is made, and it is three-quarters of the business. Over the last year every ₦1,000 spent on Meta in Nigeria brought back about ₦8,900 of sales, while the same ₦1,000 in the UK, Canada or the US brought back ₦3,300 to ₦3,900. Nigeria is 75% of sales and the only market where ads clearly pay.

Growth has stalled and each naira now buys less than it did. Sales from July to September were ₦269M, below the same months last year at ₦289M, even though we spent nearly three times as much on ads as we did then. In February every ₦1,000 on Meta brought back ₦8,400 of sales; by September it brought back ₦3,900. September was the biggest spending month of the year and bought fewer new Nigerian customers than April did on ₦1.6M less.

The ad money has been spread too thin for Meta to learn from it. We ran 82 campaigns a month this year, most on ₦10,000 to ₦15,000 a day, and a third of the last quarter's spend sat in campaigns that bought fewer than seven sales in the month. The same Lagos buyers saw our ads eight to eleven times a month in April, May, August and September, while ads that were working were switched off and replaced with new ones that started learning from zero.

Our ads keep finding people who already buy from us, which hides what a new customer really costs. Past buyers are not excluded from any prospecting campaign and targeting is left wide open, so part of every budget goes to existing customers. Meta says a Nigerian sale cost about ₦19,400 last quarter; counting only genuinely first-time buyers, a new Nigerian customer cost about ₦31,000, roughly 1.6 times what the reports show. In September Meta claimed 861 sales when the shop took 804 orders from every source combined.

Two products went missing from the shelf and took their sales with them. Blush Bloom was 18% of sales last year and is 1% now, with no stock in Lagos; Seduction has none either; Sweet Oud, which was 16% of UK sales and 19% of Canadian sales last year, has two bottles in each of those warehouses. Some of the fall in June and July was demand we could not serve.

The best creative we own is the same in every channel: a real person, one feeling, the product in passing. On Meta, ads that open on a feeling such as "Romance in a bottle" or "compliment magnet" brought back ₦32 to ₦72 per ₦1, while ads that open with a description of the notes sit at the bottom. On TikTok, a named woman on screen for under 20 seconds reaches the most new people and gets 6.6% engagement, while long reviews and "origin and notes" videos are finished by fewer than 2% of viewers. Our customers have already written the lines: 991 reviews, 313 of them usable word for word, sorted by the kind of buyer each one speaks to.

Organic content converts better than paid and we have been running it blind. Organic social brought 15% of visits and 36% of purchases this year, more than twice the conversion rate of paid social, and Instagram is credited with 59% of orders. Yet TikTok reach per post has fallen from about 1,200 people in November 2025 to about 300 in July as posting became sporadic and switched to editorial skits, and Instagram organic is not connected to any reporting at all.

Men are cheaper to win and get a tenth of the money. Men are 11% of spend and 12% of sales at about ₦20,200 a sale, and men aged 25 to 34 are the second-cheapest audience in the whole account at ₦17,300. Women aged 35 to 54 take 38% of spend at ₦27,700 to ₦29,700 a sale, the dearest audience we buy. There has been one small men's campaign in two years.

Overseas shoppers want the product and balk at the bill. They add to cart more readily than Nigerians, then drop off between cart and checkout (77% carry on in the UK, 75% in the US, 97% in Nigeria) and again at payment, where only 16% to 18% of overseas checkouts finish. Every overseas order pays a flat delivery fee, no market has a free-delivery threshold, and reviews mention the total cost and the absence of a returns policy. A new customer now costs ₦95,000 in the UK and ₦80,000 in Canada, against break-even of ₦81,000 and ₦78,000.

The peak is mid-October and last year's Black Friday was never used. The week of 15 to 21 October 2025 sold 99 orders a day, the best week in the company's history; Black Friday weekend, with no offer, no code and no email, sold 31 a day against a November average of 35, and the week before Christmas was the second peak. The season rewards us when we show up for it.

Email reaches less than half the people who walk away, and the rebuild tripled the mail without adding orders. Only 42% of started checkouts get an abandoned-checkout email, and that one flow earns four times more per email than any other. Since the May rebuild we have sent three times as many emails for the same 100 or so orders, reviews fell from 98 a month to 11 once the review request moved into the new flow, and the Black Friday email opened at 9.8%.
2. HOW WE WILL GROW

Buy genuinely new customers in Nigeria, and only step up when it pays. Past buyers come out of every prospecting ad. Five campaigns replace eighty, each with a budget big enough to learn, with separate ad sets for women 25 to 34, women 35 and over, men 25 to 44, a catalogue campaign and, from December, gift buyers. Spend rises in 25% steps every fortnight from 1 November, from about ₦14M a month toward ₦35M to ₦40M, paying up to ₦46,000 for each new customer against a break-even of ₦66,000; a step is taken only if the previous fortnight held. Aim: about 2,600 new Nigerian customers.

Make content the engine, not the afterthought. Twelve or more new pieces a month, every one built as one buyer, one feeling, one hero product and one customer's line; real women on screen, under 20 seconds, the product shown rather than explained. Long reviews, notes explainers and photo posts stop as standalone posts. The best organic posts become the ads; the best ads become the posts.

Build a creator engine that feeds both. Fifteen Nigerian creators a month and two each in the UK, Canada and the US, each with product, a tracked link and the right to run their video as an ad on Meta and TikTok. The honest-review format brought back ₦11,200 of sales per ₦1,000 in Nigeria; overseas creators are chosen for their city, not their heritage, because Nigerian creative did not travel. Aim: eight or more creator videos running as ads every month.

Bring TikTok back to life, then test it as a paid channel. Four organic posts a week in the format that reaches new people, from 19 October, so that reach climbs back above 1,200 a post by the end of November. From 1 November, Nigeria only, the ten best creator videos are boosted each month as Spark Ads, with a stop rule at ₦66,000 per new customer after four weeks.

Give the founder a job. Ihuoma's face already sells in Nigeria, where her Passion ad brought back ₦22 per ₦1, so she stays on camera here. Abroad she works through press, podcasts and events, each with a way to buy and a tracked link, because the same founder ads got no sales in the UK, Canada or the US.

Bring customers back through our own channels rather than paying for them twice. Email that reaches the inbox, abandoned-checkout coverage lifted from 42% toward 70%, a "your next scent" email 25 to 75 days after a first order, SMS and WhatsApp, and a VIP list for Black November. Aim: 40% more repeat orders than today's pace, a target rather than a forecast, since last year repeat orders rose 4% from Q3 to Q4.

Make the season count, starting with the week we are in. Protect 15 to 25 October with stock and funded campaigns. Black November, 20 to 30 November: a free gift with every order, one code per market so we can count it, judged against last year's 124 orders. Christmas, 1 to 24 December: gift sets and gift wrap, with men's gifting ads from 10 November and order-by dates published by 15 November. Aim: November and December 40% above today's pace.

Grow abroad only where it pays, and fix the checkout first. One campaign per country on local audiences and local creators, with Canada running a four-week heritage control at a quarter of its budget. Delivery time and the full cost shown before checkout, a free-delivery threshold tested at £75 and C$100, Sweet Oud back on the shelf in both countries, and never a naira above break-even per new customer.

Turn more visitors into buyers everywhere. Four in five started checkouts die in every market; a one-page checkout and delivery cost shown early are the cheapest growth we have. A scent quiz, a gift-sets page, the refund promise on every product page, and a sample in every first order once the samples exist.
